title: Paragraph / section function Practice 2
description: 4 short texts - 8 focused paragraph / section function questions
subject: rla
passage:
TEXT A - Cafe Reuse

A campus plan describes disposable-cup waste, then proposes a deposit system for reusable cups. A later paragraph explains how cups would be returned, washed, and recirculated.

TEXT B - Noise Study

A workplace article says open offices can support quick collaboration. The next paragraph summarizes employee complaints about concentration and phone noise.

TEXT C - Garden Soil

A guide defines compost as decomposed organic material. The next paragraph lists food scraps, dry leaves, and grass clippings that can be used to make it.

TEXT D - Ferry Schedule

A notice explains that winter storms may delay ferries. The final paragraph tells passengers where to check live departure updates before traveling to the terminal.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of this paragraph or section?
questions.explanation: After the plan proposes a deposit system, the later paragraph explains the return, washing, and recirculation process.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: restates the original problem of disposable-cup waste
options.whyWrong: The waste problem motivates the proposal; the target paragraph explains operation.

options.text: explains how the proposed reusable-cup system would operate
argues that reusable cups have no costs or practical limits
options.whyWrong: Describing a process does not claim the system is cost-free or flawless.

options.text: compares two different deposit prices before choosing one
options.whyWrong: The paragraph describes the cycle of cups, not competing price options.

questions.prompt: How does this part contribute to the larger text?
questions.explanation: The paragraph develops the solution by showing what happens to cups after use.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: It abandons the proposal and returns only to describing disposable waste.
options.whyWrong: The target continues developing the proposed solution.

options.text: It supplies evidence that students already prefer reusable cups.
options.whyWrong: No preference data is described.

options.text: It moves from proposing the system to showing the practical process needed to carry it out.
It introduces an unrelated discussion of campus food prices.
options.whyWrong: The paragraph stays focused on the cup-reuse system.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of this paragraph or section?
questions.explanation: The complaints about concentration and phone noise qualify the earlier claim that open offices can support quick collaboration.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: gives a second example of how open offices improve collaboration
options.whyWrong: Complaints about concentration and noise are drawbacks, not collaboration benefits.

options.text: explains why employees prefer making phone calls in shared spaces
options.whyWrong: The paragraph reports phone noise as a complaint, not a preference.

options.text: defines the architectural features of an open office
options.whyWrong: The target focuses on employee experience, not a definition of the office layout.

options.text: introduces a drawback that complicates the earlier benefit of open offices

questions.prompt: How does this part contribute to the larger text?
questions.explanation: The paragraph helps readers evaluate the tradeoff rather than seeing only the collaboration benefit.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: It balances the earlier benefit by showing a cost of the same office design.
It proves open offices reduce productivity for every employee.
options.whyWrong: Employee complaints do not establish a universal productivity effect.

options.text: It changes the topic from office design to telephone technology.
options.whyWrong: Phone noise is evidence about the office environment, not a new technology topic.

options.text: It repeats the collaboration claim in different words.
options.whyWrong: The target introduces a limitation rather than repeating the benefit.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of this paragraph or section?
questions.explanation: The food scraps, leaves, and grass clippings make the definition easier to understand by showing what materials fit it.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: introduces a different definition that contradicts the first paragraph
options.whyWrong: The examples support the definition rather than replacing it.

options.text: provides concrete examples that clarify the definition of compost
explains the chemical stages of decomposition in chronological order
options.whyWrong: The paragraph lists materials; it does not describe decomposition stages.

options.text: argues that every type of household waste belongs in compost
options.whyWrong: A few valid examples do not imply all household waste is compostable.

questions.prompt: How does this part contribute to the larger text?
questions.explanation: The paragraph develops understanding by turning an abstract definition into concrete instances.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: It changes the definition from decomposed material to fresh food waste.
options.whyWrong: Examples of inputs do not change the definition of the finished material.

options.text: It compares compost with several commercial fertilizers.
options.whyWrong: No fertilizer comparison is described.

options.text: It gives disposal instructions for materials that cannot be composted.
options.whyWrong: The examples identify usable materials rather than disposal rules.

options.text: The examples connect the definition to familiar materials readers can recognize.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of this paragraph or section?
questions.explanation: After explaining that storms may disrupt ferries, the final paragraph tells passengers how to check live updates before traveling.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: explains the weather conditions that create winter storms
options.whyWrong: The target gives an action for passengers, not a meteorological explanation.

options.text: summarizes every ferry route and departure time for the season
options.whyWrong: The paragraph points readers to live updates rather than listing the full schedule.

options.text: gives passengers practical guidance based on the earlier risk of storm delays
argues that passengers should avoid ferries throughout the winter
options.whyWrong: Possible delays lead to checking updates, not avoiding ferries altogether.

questions.prompt: How does this part contribute to the larger text?
questions.explanation: The final paragraph makes the notice useful by connecting the risk to a specific response.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: It turns a warning about possible delays into an action passengers can take before leaving for the terminal.
It guarantees that checking the website will prevent all ferry delays.
options.whyWrong: Live information can help passengers plan; it cannot prevent storms or delays.

options.text: It shifts the notice from ferry service to general winter travel advice.
options.whyWrong: The guidance remains specific to ferry departures.

options.text: It explains why the terminal was built in its current location.
options.whyWrong: Terminal location is not part of the stated guidance.

curriculum.learningObjective: Apply paragraph / section function reasoning across varied original texts and explain answers from textual evidence.
